metadata.summary: This literature review and expert consensus examines surgical outcomes of decompression alone versus decompression with fusion for degenerative lumbar spondylolisthesis. It considers evidence from randomized trials, meta-analyses, and a radiographic cohort study, including factors that may indicate postoperative instability. Because the studies reach differing conclusions, the recommendations address how clinical features and preoperative imaging may inform the choice of operation.

target_population: Patients with degenerative lumbar spondylolisthesis being considered for surgical treatment
Patients with lumbar spinal stenosis with or without degenerative lumbar spondylolisthesis

toxicities.incidence: In the Austevoll trial, mean blood loss was 429 mL with D + F versus 141 mL with D alone (P < 0.05).
In the Austevoll trial, dural tears occurred in 13.3% of the D + F group versus 5.3% of the D alone group (P < 0.05).

toxicities.event: Reoperation at the index level for clinical or presumed instability
toxicities.incidence: In the Ghogawala trial, the cumulative reoperation rate was 34% with D alone versus 14% with D + F (P = 0.05); every revision in the D alone group was performed at the index level because of subsequent clinical instability. In the Blumenthal study, 15 (37%) patients underwent reoperation during a mean follow-up of 3.6 years. Reoperation rates after D alone were 45% with disc height >6.5 mm, 39% with facet angle >50°, and 54% with segmental motion >1.25 mm; the rate was 75% when all three factors were present and 0% when none was present.
recognition: Mechanical back pain was the reason for reoperation in the Blumenthal study.
prevention: The review advises assessing preoperative imaging for markers of instability to help identify patients who may benefit from adding fusion to a planned decompression.

toxicities.event: Reoperation at an adjacent lumbar level
toxicities.incidence: In the Ghogawala trial, the cumulative reoperation rate with D + F was 14% versus 34% with D alone (P = 0.05); every revision in the D + F group took place at an adjacent lumbar level.
In the Austevoll trial, mean hospital stay was 5 days with D + F versus 3.3 days with D alone (P < 0.05). The Ghogawala and Forsth trials also reported longer stays with fusion.
In the Austevoll trial, mean operation duration was 174 minutes with D + F versus 104 minutes with D alone (P < 0.05). The Ghogawala trial also reported longer procedures with fusion.

therapies_index.name: D alone
approved_indications: An option for surgical treatment of DLS; the review favors it as an initial surgical choice for patients with MRI-confirmed spinal stenosis, neurogenic claudication or lower-limb radicular symptoms, and degenerative spondylolisthesis of at least 3 mm on standing radiographs.
The review considers it an option for low-grade DS, while advising consideration of fusion when preoperative instability is present.
key_toxicities: In the SLIP trial, revisions after D alone occurred at the index level because of subsequent clinical instability.
The Gadjradj review reported greater postoperative slip progression and instability after D alone than after D + F.

therapies_index.name: D + F
approved_indications: An option for surgical treatment of DLS; the review advises considering fusion particularly when imaging suggests preoperative instability or when baseline disability and back pain are greater.
For patients with grade 1 spondylolisthesis, the review states that fusion may be considered to improve physical function.
key_toxicities: Compared with D alone, the reviewed studies associated D + F with greater blood loss, longer operations and hospital stays, and greater morbidity or complication rates.
The Austevoll trial reported a higher incidence of dural tears with D + F than with D alone.
In the SLIP trial, revisions after D + F occurred at an adjacent lumbar level.

therapies_index.name: laminectomy alone
approved_indications: The SLIP trial studied it in patients with symptomatic grade I DLS without instability.

therapies_index.name: midline sparing decompression surgery
approved_indications: The review conditionally recommends it for spinal stenosis with predominant leg pain.

therapies_index.name: complete laminectomy with partial removal of the medial facet joint
approved_indications: The SLIP trial used this decompression technique in patients with symptomatic grade I DLS without instability.

therapies_index.name: instrumented fusion
approved_indications: The Austevoll trial studied it alongside decompression in patients with lumbar spinal stenosis and spondylolisthesis of 3 mm or more.
therapies_index.administration: In the Austevoll trial, the fusion group received pedicle screws and rods; an intervertebral fusion device was optional.
monitoring: In the Austevoll trial, fusion was assessed by computed tomography by 2 surgeons and a radiologist; the criteria for determining fusion status were not reported.

therapies_index.name: bone graft harvested from the iliac crest
therapies_index.administration: The SLIP trial used this graft in the D + F group.

therapies_index.name: conservative care
therapies_index.administration: All patients in the Austevoll trial had 3 months of conservative care before surgery.

conditions.name: degenerative lumbar spondylolisthesis (DLS)
conditions.description: The document treats DLS as a heterogeneous condition in which stability and the possibility of instability after decompression affect surgical decisions.
conditions.epidemiology: DLS is described as common in an aging population; no incidence or prevalence estimate is provided.
conditions.clinical_presentation: In the cited surgical studies, patients had lumbar stenosis with neurogenic claudication or lower-limb radicular symptoms; some also had back pain.

subtypes.name: stable degenerative spondylolisthesis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The cited studies generally defined stability as less than 3 mm of motion on flexion-extension imaging.

subtypes.name: unstable DLS
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Existing instability may influence the decision to add fusion. One cited trial excluded translation of >3 mm on flexion-extension radiographs.

subtypes.name: potentially unstable
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The document uses this description for DLS that may become unstable after decompression alone, without establishing a definitive diagnostic definition.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess lumbar stenosis and nerve-root involvement.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Used in the cited studies to confirm stenosis before surgery.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: One cited trial defined foraminal stenosis by deformation of the nerve root on MRI; those patients were excluded from that trial.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Used to establish eligibility in the cited NORDSTEN-DS trial.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: That trial required degenerative spondylolisthesis of at least 3 mm.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess dynamic translation or segmental motion.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Considered when evaluating stability before surgical treatment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Cited studies described stable disease as less than 3 mm of motion. In the Blumenthal cohort treated with decompression alone, motion of more than 1.25 mm was associated with a 54% reoperation rate.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure disc height and facet angle as possible indicators of later instability.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Evaluated in the cited Blumenthal cohort before decompression alone.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: In that cohort, disc height >6.5 mm was associated with reoperation in 45%, and facet angle >50° with a 39% reoperation rate. The document notes methodological limitations affecting generalizability.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess radiographic features including vertebral slip and segmental motion.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Used for radiographic measurements in the cited Blumenthal cohort.

definitions.description: In the SLIP trial eligibility criteria, this grade encompassed a slip of 3 to 14 mm.

staging.additional_rules: The document does not provide a complete grading system.

conditions.name: stable degenerative spondylolisthesis
conditions.description: A form of degenerative spondylolisthesis without the dynamic motion used to define instability in the cited studies. Absence of that motion did not eliminate the possibility of later instability after decompression alone.
conditions.clinical_presentation: The cited cohorts included patients with neurogenic claudication; one study also required the absence of severe mechanical back pain.

subtypes.name: stable Grade I spondylolisthesis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The Blumenthal cohort required less than 3 mm of motion on flexion-extension radiographs and no severe mechanical back pain.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure dynamic motion and assess stability.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Used before enrollment in the cited studies of stable disease.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Stability was defined as less than 3 mm of motion in the cited studies. In the Blumenthal decompression-alone cohort, motion of more than 1.25 mm was associated with a 54% reoperation rate.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure disc height and facet angle.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Used for these measurements in the cited Blumenthal study.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Among patients treated with decompression alone, disc height >6.5 mm was associated with reoperation in 45%, while facet angle >50° was associated with a 39% reoperation rate.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure radiographic parameters other than the disc height and facet angle assessed on CT in the cited Blumenthal study.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Used in that study's preoperative assessment.

definitions.description: The cited Blumenthal study examined patients with this grade, but the document does not give its measurement-based definition for that cohort.

conditions.name: unstable DLS
conditions.description: Degenerative spondylolisthesis with instability, distinguished from stable disease when considering whether decompression should be accompanied by fusion.
conditions.clinical_presentation: A history of mechanical low back pain with axial loading was one surgeon-assessed reason for excluding patients from the cited SLIP trial because of suspected lumbar instability.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Used to assess instability in cited surgical studies.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The SLIP trial excluded patients with >3 mm translation. The document notes that other studies did not consistently analyze patients with dynamic instability separately.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Look for radiographic signs of instability when deciding whether fusion may be appropriate.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Before selecting surgical treatment for DLS.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The document presents disc height, facet angle and segmental motion as possible indicators, while cautioning that the study supporting specific thresholds had limited generalizability.

conditions.name: lumbar spinal stenosis
conditions.description: Lumbar narrowing studied both in patients with DLS and in patients without DLS; the document discusses how that distinction affects interpretation of surgical evidence.
conditions.clinical_presentation: The cited studies included pseudoclaudication or neurogenic claudication, lower-limb radicular symptoms, and back or leg pain.

subtypes.name: lumbar spinal stenosis with degenerative spondylolisthesis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Stenosis accompanied by degenerative vertebral slip.

subtypes.name: lumbar spinal stenosis without DLS
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Stenosis without the degenerative spondylolisthesis used to stratify patients in the cited SSSS trial.

subtypes.name: foraminal stenosis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: In the cited NORDSTEN-DS trial, this was defined by nerve-root deformation on MRI, and affected patients were excluded.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Confirm stenosis and evaluate the affected segments.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Used in the eligibility assessments of the cited stenosis trials.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The SSSS trial required 1 or 2 adjacent stenotic segments between L2-S1 with dural-sac cross-sectional area ≤75 mm2. The NORDSTEN-DS trial confirmed stenosis on MRI.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Determine whether degenerative spondylolisthesis accompanies stenosis.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Used for enrollment in the cited NORDSTEN-DS trial.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: That trial required degenerative spondylolisthesis of at least 3 mm.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess dynamic motion when stenosis coexists with DLS.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Used to characterize patients in the cited studies.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The NORDSTEN-DS trial included patients with dynamic motion but did not analyze them separately from patients with stable DLS.

recommendations.statement: Fusion may be considered instead of laminectomy alone to improve physical function in patients with grade 1 spondylolisthesis.
recommendations.rationale: The SLIP trial found greater improvement in physical health with fusion, but fusion also increased surgical morbidity.

recommendations.statement: Patients with spinal stenosis and predominant leg pain should undergo midline sparing decompression surgery.
recommendations.rationale: The SSSS trial found no additional clinical benefit from fusion, although uncertainty about patient selection limits how broadly its findings can be applied.

recommendations.statement: Both D and D + F are surgical options for patients with DLS.
recommendations.rationale: The SSSS trial did not establish which patients with DLS are best suited to either approach; fusion may be appropriate in selected patients likely to develop postoperative instability.

recommendations.statement: Offer midline sparing decompression alone as the first surgical choice for patients with MRI-confirmed spinal stenosis, neurogenic claudication or lower-limb radicular symptoms, and degenerative spondylolisthesis measuring at least 3 mm on standing radiographs.
recommendations.context: Surgical treatment after 3 months of conservative care in the NORDSTEN-DS trial population.
recommendations.rationale: D alone was non-inferior to D + F for ODI reduction at 2-year after surgery.
recommendations.source_heading: Recommendation regarding Impact on Clinical Practice

recommendations.statement: Consider decompression alone a non-inferior treatment option to decompression with fusion for low-grade DS.
recommendations.rationale: The reviewed studies found no difference in functional, pain or clinical outcomes at two years of follow-up, while decompression alone was associated with less blood loss, shorter stays and fewer complications.

recommendations.statement: Consider fusion for patients with low-grade DS who show signs of preoperative instability.
recommendations.context: Selection of surgery for low-grade DS.
recommendations.rationale: The reviewed studies observed greater slip progression after decompression alone.

recommendations.statement: For the majority of patients with DLS, surgeons should give equal consideration to D and D + F.
recommendations.rationale: The review found similar raw outcome scores at final follow-up, while methodological concerns limit confidence in its finding of greater improvement with fusion.

recommendations.statement: Consider offering fusion to patients with DLS who have greater baseline disability and back pain.
recommendations.rationale: The review reported greater improvement from baseline with fusion, but the reason for greater baseline disability in that group was unclear.

recommendations.statement: Evaluate radiographic parameters to help determine whether fusion should be added to a planned decompression for DLS.
recommendations.context: Preoperative assessment for surgical treatment of DLS.
recommendations.rationale: A small study linked segmental motion >1.25 mm, disc height >6.5 mm and facet angle >50° to reoperation after decompression alone; its methodological limitations restrict generalizability.

recommendations.statement: Both D alone and DF may be considered for the surgical management of DLS.
recommendations.rationale: The reviewed evidence does not establish which approach is appropriate for every patient; fusion adds morbidity and may be most justified when instability warrants it.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients being considered for surgical treatment of DLS.
decision_rules: Both D alone and D + F may be considered; the evidence does not establish one approach as suitable for every patient with DLS.
Examine preoperative imaging for signs of instability when deciding whether fusion is warranted.
Consider the additional morbidity of fusion against the risk of instability after decompression alone.

recommended_regimens.name: D alone
recommended_regimens.summary: An acceptable surgical option for selected patients with DLS.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The reviewed RCTs found no difference in ODI at final follow-up between D alone and D + F, but differed in their findings on reoperation.

recommended_regimens.name: D + F
recommended_regimens.summary: An acceptable surgical option for selected patients with DLS, particularly when instability makes decompression alone less suitable.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The reviewed studies reached conflicting conclusions about comparative functional outcomes and reoperation; fusion entails additional surgical morbidity.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document does not establish precise criteria that determine which patients require fusion. Differences in populations and surgical techniques limit broad application of individual study findings.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with grade 1 spondylolisthesis being considered for decompressive laminectomy; the supporting SLIP trial enrolled patients with symptomatic grade I DLS without instability, defined as less than 3 mm motion on dynamic radiographs.
decision_rules: Fusion may be considered alongside laminectomy to improve physical function, while accounting for its greater morbidity.

recommended_regimens.name: D + F
recommended_regimens.summary: Fusion may be added to laminectomy for improvement in physical function; this is a conditional option, not a requirement for all patients.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In the SLIP trial, the increase in SF-36 physical-component summary score at 2 years was 15.2 with D + F versus 9.5 with D alone (difference 5.7, 95% CI 0.1 to 11.3, P = 0.046); the between-group difference at 4 years was 6.7 points (P = 0.02). Cumulative reoperation rates were 14% with D + F versus 34% with D alone (P = 0.05). The between-group difference in ODI reduction at 2 years was not significant (P = 0.06).

alternative_regimens.name: D alone
alternative_regimens.summary: Laminectomy without fusion was the comparator in the SLIP trial; its revisions occurred at the index level after subsequent clinical instability.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Selection should account for the patient's risk of postoperative instability and the greater morbidity of fusion.

response_assessment.method: SF-36 physical-component summary score and ODI
response_assessment.interpretation: These were outcomes assessed in the SLIP trial, not a prescribed clinical follow-up schedule.

response_assessment.method: SF-36 physical-component summary score and reoperation
response_assessment.interpretation: The SLIP trial reported sustained physical-function differences and cumulative reoperations through follow-up.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: In the SLIP trial, D + F involved greater blood loss, longer procedures and longer hospital stays than D alone (P < 0.001). All revisions in its fusion group occurred at an adjacent lumbar level. The document cautions that fusion may be unsuitable for some patients with comorbidities and that outcomes after less invasive decompression were not established by this trial.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with spinal stenosis and predominant leg pain.
decision_rules: Offer a decompression that preserves the midline structures.

recommended_regimens.name: midline sparing decompression surgery
recommended_regimens.summary: The SSSS-based recommendation conditionally favors this decompression approach when leg pain predominates.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In the SSSS, D + F and D-alone groups had no statistically significant differences in the reported PROMs, 6-min walking test or reoperation rates at the assessed follow-up points, including after stratification by presence of DLS.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The SSSS enrolled patients both with and without DLS, and its surgical techniques were not standardized. The document therefore cautions against applying its findings to every patient with DLS.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with DLS and spinal stenosis for whom either decompression or decompression with fusion is being considered.
decision_rules: Both D and D + F are options.
Consider whether postoperative instability is likely before accepting the added morbidity of fusion.

recommended_regimens.name: D
recommended_regimens.summary: Decompression without fusion remains a surgical option for appropriately selected patients with DLS.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In the SSSS, stratification by presence or absence of DLS did not reveal statistically significant between-group differences in the reported clinical outcomes or reoperation rates at two and five years.

recommended_regimens.name: D + F
recommended_regimens.summary: Decompression with fusion remains an option, including for selected patients at risk of postoperative instability.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In the SSSS, fusion was associated with significantly longer hospital stays, increased intraoperative bleeding and higher direct costs, without a demonstrated difference in the reported clinical outcomes after stratification by DLS.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The SSSS did not establish detailed indications for either operation in DLS; uncertainty about dynamic instability, foraminal stenosis and variation in operative techniques limit generalization.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with MRI-confirmed spinal stenosis accompanied by neurogenic claudication or radicular symptoms in the lower limbs, and degenerative spondylolisthesis of at least 3 mm on standing radiographs.
decision_rules: Offer decompression that preserves the midline as the first surgical choice for this population.
The supporting trial included patients with dynamic motion but did not analyze them separately; its results do not establish the best approach for that subgroup.

recommended_regimens.name: midline sparing decompression alone
recommended_regimens.summary: The NORDSTEN-DS-based recommendation conditionally offers this operation as the first surgical choice.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In the NORDSTEN-DS per-protocol analysis, 75.5% of the D alone group and 75.5% of the D + F group achieved at least 30% reduction in ODI at 2-year follow-up. Reoperation occurred in 12.5% with D alone and 9.1% with D + F; the reported difference did not reach significance (95% CI of 4.6 to 11.5).

alternative_regimens.name: D + F
alternative_regimens.summary: This was the comparator in NORDSTEN-DS; decompression alone was non-inferior for the trial's primary ODI outcome.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The document does not define a specific criterion within this trial population that requires fusion.

response_assessment.timepoint: every 3 months up to 2 years postoperatively
response_assessment.interpretation: This describes the NORDSTEN-DS assessment schedule rather than a prescribed clinical follow-up schedule.
This was the trial's primary threshold for clinically important improvement in functioning.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: NORDSTEN-DS excluded foraminal stenosis defined by nerve-root deformation on MRI. Relative to D alone, D + F had higher mean surgery duration (174 vs 104 minutes), mean hospital stay (5 days vs 3.3 days), blood loss (429 vs 141 mL) and dural-tear incidence (13.3% vs 5.3%); P < 0.05 for each. The document notes a nonsignificant trend toward greater back-pain improvement with fusion that needs further investigation.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with low-grade DS being considered for surgery, with particular attention to signs of preop instability.
decision_rules: Consider decompression alone a non-inferior treatment option relative to decompression with fusion.
Consider fusion when signs of preop instability are present, taking account of the greater slip progression observed after decompression alone in the reviewed studies.

recommended_regimens.name: D alone
recommended_regimens.summary: A conditionally supported option for low-grade DS, described as non-inferior to D + F in the reviewed outcomes.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The Gadjradj review reported no significant between-group differences in ODI, SF36, VAS or walking improvement at two years after surgery. D alone was associated with less blood loss, shorter hospital stays and lower costs, while two included studies reported statistically significant slip progression relative to D + F.

recommended_regimens.name: D + F
recommended_regimens.summary: Fusion should be considered when signs of preop instability make decompression alone less suitable.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The Gadjradj review found greater direct costs and complications with D + F, while the D-alone group had greater slip progression in the two studies that reported it.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document rates the evidence for this recommendation as Low and does not treat the review's findings as establishing one operation for every patient with low-grade DS.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with DLS, particularly those with greater baseline disability and back pain.
decision_rules: For the majority of patients, consider D and D + F equally.
Consider offering fusion to patients with greater baseline disability and back pain, while weighing its higher morbidity.

recommended_regimens.name: D
recommended_regimens.summary: One of the options to consider equally for most patients with DLS.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The Shukla review reported similar raw NRS, ODI and EQ5-D scores at final follow-up between D alone and D + F.

recommended_regimens.name: D + F
recommended_regimens.summary: One of the options for most patients with DLS; fusion may be offered particularly when baseline disability and back pain are greater.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The Shukla review reported greater improvement from preop to final follow-up in ODI and NRS leg and back pain with D + F, despite similar raw final scores. It also reported significantly longer operations and hospital stays, greater blood loss and more complications with D + F.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document identifies heterogeneity, inclusion of retrospective cohorts and uncertainty about the reasons for greater baseline disability in the fusion group as limitations of this evidence.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with DLS for whom fusion might be added to a planned decompression, including patients with radiographic features associated with reoperation after D alone.
decision_rules: Evaluate preoperative imaging for markers of instability when deciding whether to add fusion.
The Blumenthal study suggests segmental motion >1.25 mm, disc height >6.5 mm and facet angle >50° as potential risk markers; its small sample and nonstandardized outcomes limit generalization.

recommended_regimens.name: D + F
recommended_regimens.summary: Radiographic evaluation may help determine whether to add fusion to a planned decompression; the document does not require fusion at any single reported threshold.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Among patients treated with D alone in the Blumenthal study, reoperation was reported in 45% with disc height >6.5 mm, 39% with facet angle >50° and 54% with motion greater than 1.25 mm. Patients with all three risk factors had a 75% reoperation rate, compared with 0% among patients with none.

alternative_regimens.name: D alone
alternative_regimens.summary: The only operation studied in the Blumenthal cohort; its radiographic associations may inform selection but do not establish a comparative benefit from adding fusion.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider the assessed risk of postoperative instability; the study did not test a fusion arm.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The Blumenthal cohort comprised 40 patients with stable Grade I spondylolisthesis and neurogenic claudication. Reoperation for mechanical back pain presumed to reflect index-level instability occurred in 15 (37%) during a mean follow-up of 3.6 years. The document notes methodological concerns and limited generalizability.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: Study design: literature review. Objective: compare outcomes after decompression with fusion (D + F) and decompression alone (D) for degenerative lumbar spondylolisthesis (DLS). Methods: the authors selected 6 articles: 3 randomized clinical trials (RCT), 2 meta-analyses and 1 radiographic cohort study, then combined the evidence with expert clinical recommendations. Results: in Ghogawala, D + F produced better SF-36 results (P = 0.046) and fewer reoperations (P = 0.05) than D. Forsth studied stenosis with and without DLS and found no difference in reported outcomes or reoperations. Austevoll found D non-inferior to D + F for ODI reduction at 2-year after surgery. Gadjradi reported greater morbidity with D + F. Shukla found no difference in unadjusted patient outcome scores at final follow-up. Among patients receiving D in Blumenthal, disc height >6.5 mm, facet angle >50° and dynamic motion >1.25 mm were associated with reoperation rates of 45%, 39% and 54%, respectively. Conclusions: because the RCTs and meta-analyses disagree, their findings do not support a universal efficacy claim for either operation in DLS. Surgeons should examine preoperative imaging carefully for instability when selecting an operation.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: DLS is common in an aging population. Whether instrumented D + F offers advantages over D remains disputed because the evidence varies. Recent studies have examined comparative outcomes and contributors to treatment failure. This review aims to summarize that evidence and develop recommendations informed by both the studies and expert consensus.

document_sections.heading: Methods
document_sections.content: The AO Spine Knowledge Forum Degenerative steering committee chose 6 pertinent publications: three RCT’s, two meta-analyses of RCT’s and prospective cohorts, and one radiographic cohort investigating objective indicators of instability. Selection reflected data quality, recency and relevance and was at the committee’s discretion. A group of three Knowledge Forum members summarized each article; the first author consolidated the summaries, and all 23 forum members reviewed the manuscript. The final clinical recommendations were agreed after a virtual discussion of the summaries.

document_sections.heading: Study Summary
document_sections.content: The Spinal Laminectomy vs Instrumented Pedicle Screw (SLIP) randomized controlled trial compared D + F with D in symptomatic grade I DLS without instability, defined as less than 3 mm motion on dynamic radiographs. Its primary endpoint was change in the physical-component summary of SF-36 at 2 years; secondary assessment included ODI, with follow-up to 4 years. Of 66 randomized patients, mean age was 67 years, 80% were women, and 68% remained in follow-up at 4 years. At 2 years, the D + F and D groups gained 15.2 and 9.5 SF-36 points, respectively: difference 5.7, 95% CI 0.1 to 11.3, P = 0.046. The difference persisted at 3 and 4 years; at 4 years it was 6.7 points (P = 0.02). ODI reductions did not differ significantly at 2 years (P = 0.06). D + F involved more blood loss, longer operations and longer admissions than D (P < 0.001). Cumulative reoperations were 14% with D + F and 34% with D (P = 0.05); every D + F revision involved an adjacent lumbar level, whereas every D revision involved the original level because of subsequent clinical instability. The study authors interpreted fusion after laminectomy as giving a small but clinically meaningful physical-health benefit lasting up to 4 years in this population, despite greater operative and recovery burdens. Enrollment occurred at five centers between March 2002 and August 2009; 51 out of 106 patients came from one site, and predominance of academic sites could have limited generalizability or favored enrollment of more severely symptomatic patients. Eligible patients had grade I DLS measuring 3 to 14 mm, lumbar stenosis and neurogenic claudication, with or without lumbar radiculopathy. Exclusions included >3 mm translation on flexion-extension films, a surgeon’s judgment of instability based on axial-loading mechanical low-back pain, previous lumbar surgery, or American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) class IV or higher disease. Subjective exclusion for instability could cause selection bias; stenosis severity, symptom duration and earlier pain treatments were not eligibility criteria and could confound results. Two neuroradiologists and one neurosurgeon reviewed diagnostic images, and postoperative CT scans underwent independent protocol review. The estimated required sample was 64 patients (32 per group), providing 80% power to detect a 7.5-point SF-36 between-group difference at a two-sided significance level of 0.05. The analysis plan was formulated after trial completion but before examination of the data. D consisted of complete laminectomy and partial medial-facet removal; D + F additionally used pedicle screws, titanium alloy rods and iliac-crest bone graft. The trial did not assess bone morphogenetic protein (BMP), interbody devices, or minimally invasive decompression or fusion. Small, nonsignificant baseline imbalances might have affected outcomes. Changes at both 1-year and 2-year were initially primary SF-36 outcomes. Funding limits and substantial dropout shortened follow-up to 4 years rather than the planned 5-year period. The enrollment goal was 100 patients, with at least 64 randomized; funding also covered a parallel registry of 40 patients declining randomization. Wallace Clinical Trials Center managed the data without industry participation. Mailed questionnaires and repeated follow-up efforts could affect response accuracy; dropout after 4 years and retention of post-reoperation observations without censoring could weaken reliability. The sample was considered sufficient to detect meaningful quality-of-life results. Groups did not differ significantly at 1-year, but the fusion group had greater SF-36 physical-component gains at 2, 3 and 4 years, including a 6.7-point difference at 4 years (P = 0.02). The review cautions that D + F has significantly greater morbidity and may be unsuitable for patients with comorbidities. Because surgeons used complete laminectomy with partial medial facetectomies, whether a midline-preserving laminotomy/foraminotomy would lower D reoperations is unknown. Fewer overall revisions with fusion came at the cost of adjacent-level revisions. More research is needed to identify who develops postoperative instability or severe mechanical back pain and might justify fusion. The review assigns this article Moderate evidence quality and gives a Conditional recommendation that fusion may be considered instead of laminectomy alone to improve physical function in grade 1 spondylolisthesis.

document_sections.heading: Study Summary
document_sections.content: The Swedish Spinal Stenosis Study (SSSS) was a multicenter, open-label superiority trial assigning patients 1:1 to D + F or D after stratification by DLS presence. Eligibility required age 50-80 years, >6 months of pseudoclaudication in one or both legs, back-pain VAS > 30, and MRI showing 1 or 2 adjacent stenotic levels between L2-S1 with dural-sac cross-sectional area ≤75 mm2. Exclusions were spondylolysis, degenerative scoliosis, non-degenerative stenosis, herniated-disk-related stenosis, rheumatic disease, neoplasm, neurologic disorder, prior lumbar surgery, compression-fracture history at affected levels, and psychological disorders precluding appropriate participation. ODI was primary; secondary outcomes included EQ-5D, back- and leg-pain VAS and ZCQ. Four further questions addressed satisfaction, overall back and leg pain, and walking. Postal PROMs were collected before surgery and at 2 and 5 years; a 6-minute walk test was performed at baseline and 2 years. Medical records supplied complication and reoperation information, and direct and indirect costs were calculated. Among 228 treated patients completing 2-year follow-up, 111 received D + F (67 with DLS) and 117 received D (66 with DLS). At 5 years, information was available for 138: 65 after D + F (39 with DLS) and 73 after D (41 with DLS). Baseline and preoperative characteristics did not differ significantly. At two and five years, the groups did not differ statistically in any of nine PROMs, the 6-min walk test, indirect costs, complications or reoperations; stratification by DLS did not change that result. A post hoc subgroup with slip of 7.4 to 14.3 mm likewise showed no ODI or VAS difference at baseline or 2 years. Fusion did, however, significantly increase admission length, intraoperative blood loss and direct costs. The study authors concluded that adding fusion provided no additional clinical benefit for lumbar stenosis, including stenosis with DLS. Stratified randomization supported group balance, and web-based allocation reduced selection bias. The review notes that inclusion of patients without spondylolisthesis has been questioned: trauma, tumor and deformity were excluded, while other possible reasons for fusion, such as foraminal stenosis or severe mechanical back pain, were not characterized. This uncertainty complicates comparisons with DLS-only studies and limits generalization. Surgeons selected techniques without prespecified standardization; posterolateral, interbody and non-instrumented fusion, and central or midline-preserving decompression, introduced heterogeneity. The trial documented participant flow with CONSORT and collected perioperative data through Swespine; follow-up at two and five years and a per-protocol primary analysis were additional strengths, although that analysis excluded patients who did not receive assigned treatment or were lost. Stratified and exploratory post-hoc analyses were performed, and missing health-economic data underwent multiple imputation. Cost information nevertheless came from only one center and may not reflect other settings. Patient costs were not collected beyond two years, potentially omitting costs of many fusion reoperations because mean reoperation time was 37 months; supporting health-economic data were absent from both manuscript and appendices. Mixed DLS status, variable operations and uncertainty about dynamic instability and foraminal stenosis prevent broad application to every patient with DLS. A less invasive D strategy may suit appropriately selected patients, but the trial did not establish its precise indications; fusion morbidity may be justified when postoperative instability is likely. The review rates evidence quality Moderate and makes a Conditional recommendation for midline-sparing decompression in spinal stenosis with predominant leg pain, while regarding both D and D + F as options in DLS.

document_sections.heading: Study Summary
document_sections.content: The Austevoll open-label, multicenter noninferiority trial compared single-level D and D + F for lumbar stenosis with spondylolisthesis of 3 mm or more. Its null hypothesis specified that the proportion achieving at least a 30% ODI reduction with D would be at least 15 percentage points lower than with D + F; this ODI change represented clinically important functional improvement. Participants were 18 to 80 years old, with mean age 66 years, MRI-confirmed stenosis and either neurogenic claudication or lower-limb radicular symptoms, plus degenerative slip of at least 3 mm on standing films. Dynamic flexion-extension motion was permitted but was neither a stratification factor nor analyzed separately. Foraminal stenosis, defined by MRI-visible nerve-root deformation, was an exclusion. All patients received 3 months of conservative care. Assignment to D or instrumented D + F was 1:1, and all decompressions spared the midline. Assessments occurred every 3 months through 2 years. Of 267 recruited patients, 134 were assigned D and 133 D + F; 89.9% of the 267 patients (240 patients) had 2-year data. In the per-protocol primary analysis, 75.5% in each group achieved at least a 30% ODI reduction. ZCQ symptom severity, physical function and satisfaction; NRS back and leg pain; global perceived scale; and EQ-5D showed no significant between-group differences. D + F versus D had greater mean surgery duration (174 vs 104 minutes), mean admission length (5 days vs 3.3 days), blood loss (429 vs 141 mL) and dural-tear incidence (13.3% vs 5.3%); each comparison had P < 0.05. Reoperations occurred in 12.5% after D and 9.1% after D + F, without statistical significance (95% CI of 4.6 to 11.5). Other medical and surgical complication rates did not differ significantly. The study’s Table 2 suggested greater improvements in NRS leg and back pain after D + F, but neither trend was statistically significant. The authors reported preoperative dynamic instability in 20% without separate analysis, leaving its effect uncertain. They noted the study lacked power to establish whether the reoperation difference was significant. Randomization and data collection were considered robust. Midline structures were preserved with D but not with D + F, which used pedicle screws and rods; an intervertebral device was optional (38% incidence). Two surgeons and a radiologist assessed fusion on CT without reported fusion-status criteria. Recruitment met statistical-power needs, and both intention-to-treat and per-protocol analyses were conducted. Exclusion of patients needing reoperation from the per-protocol analysis probably favored D.

document_sections.heading: Recommendation regarding Impact on Clinical Practice
document_sections.content: D met the trial’s noninferiority criterion against D + F for ODI reduction at 2-year after surgery. A later report on this cohort gave similar 5-year results. The nonsignificant trend toward greater back-pain improvement with fusion needs further study. The review judges the evidence High and issues a Conditional recommendation to offer midline-sparing D as the initial surgical choice for patients with MRI-confirmed stenosis, neurogenic claudication or lower-limb radicular symptoms, and degenerative spondylolisthesis of at least 3 mm on standing radiographs.

document_sections.heading: Study Summary
document_sections.content: Gadjradj and colleagues systematically compared D with D + F for DLS. Their search identified 2403 studies and included 7: 5 RCT’s and 2 prospective studies. Meta-analysis found no significant difference at two years in ODI, SF36, VAS or walking improvement. D entailed significantly less blood loss, shorter admissions and lower costs, with a similar reoperation rate; D + F had higher direct costs and more complications. In the two studies reporting slip progression, progression was statistically significantly greater after D. Most included studies had low or unclear selection-bias risk and focused on low-grade DS. The authors followed PRISMA and registered a Prospero protocol, CRD42021291603. Their search involved an experienced librarian and stated eligibility criteria. Posterior decompression and/or fusion approaches performed before, after or during the same surgical session were eligible; surgeons selected fusion devices, grafts and instrumentation, allowing flexibility but also possible confounding. Only three different techniques were used through a minimally invasive approach, limiting representation of broader practice. Data and outcomes were independently extracted, with disagreements settled by consensus. Cochrane Collaboration criteria were applied to selection, performance, attrition, detection and selective-reporting bias in RCTs; prospective studies were not assessed because higher bias was expected. The review observes that instruments for assessing nonrandomized studies exist and that, with so few studies, the bias status of the two prospective studies matters to evidence quality under GRADE. Analyses used RCTs only, potentially excluding useful data despite the limited and relatively bias-prone evidence base. Continuous outcomes were expressed as mean differences with 95% confidence intervals, and reoperation as odds ratios. Random-effects analyses used the DerSimonian and Laird approach; heterogeneity was inspected in Forest plots and assessed with the Q-test (chi-square) and I2. GRADE assessed evidence across design limitations, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and factors including publication bias. Applying AMSTAR2, the review authors judged the systematic review’s evidence level LOW. The meta-analysis found comparable function, pain and clinical outcomes for low-grade DLS at two years, with less blood loss, shorter stays and fewer complications after D. D + F might limit slip progression; postoperative instability was more frequent after D in the review. The present review assigns Low evidence quality and gives a Conditional recommendation to consider D non-inferior to D + F for low-grade DS, while considering fusion when preoperative instability signs are present because greater slip progression was observed after D.

document_sections.heading: Study Summary
document_sections.content: The PRISMA-based Shukla review comprised 90 996 DLS patients across 23 studies: 10 267 (11.3%) received D and 80 729 (88.7%) D + F. D + F significantly increased operative time, admission duration, blood loss and complications, while final unadjusted NRS, ODI and EQ5-D scores were similar. From baseline to final follow-up, ODI and NRS leg- and back-pain improvements were greater with D + F in both the full sample and the stable-spondylolisthesis subgroup, where stability meant less than 3 mm motion on flexion-extension x-rays. The study authors therefore inferred greater functional improvement with D + F for stable and unstable DLS. Searches covered English-language publications in PubMed, Scopus and EMBASE through August 6, 2022, from database inception. RCTs and cohorts with at least 5 patients were eligible. Primary outcomes included hospital-stay duration, reoperation, major complications, ODI change, and leg- and back-pain NRS change. Analyses examined all studies together, RCTs alone and stable-spondylolisthesis studies alone. The authors used standard mean difference (SMD) to compare differently collected outcomes, emphasizing change from baseline. For ODI improvement, D + F was favored (SMD: 0.38, 95% CI: [ 0.57, 0.19], P < 0.01); corresponding results were NRS Leg SMD: 0.11, 95% CI: [ 0.21, 0.01], P = 0.04, and NRS Back pain SMD: 0.45, 95% CI: [ 0.66, 0.23], P < 0.01. The study authors argued that patients receiving fusion began with more disability and worse ODI and NRS pain; similar final scores could therefore represent greater improvement. In stable spondylolisthesis, complications did not differ (OR: 1.12, 95% CI: [0.34, 3.65], P = 0.86), ODI change was greater with D + F (SMD: 0.57, 95% CI: [ 0.98, 0.17], P = 0.0054), and the trend toward fewer fusion reoperations was not significant (OR: 0.53, 95% CI: [0.28, 1.29], P = 0.063). In the RCT-only subgroup, inconsistent reporting prevented pooled functional analysis; two studies showed nonsignificant trends toward greater functional improvement. Pooled RCT complication data showed more complications with D + F. Limitations include failure to list excluded publications and heterogeneity in populations, instability measurement, DLS grade and procedures. Inconsistent RCT reporting prevented pooled analysis of level 1 functional data. Meta-analyses of intraoperative variables, reoperations, ODI and NRS back pain had high heterogeneity (I2 > 40%); combined with small effect sizes, this raises concern about the reliability of the conclusions. AMSTAR2 yielded a LOW evidence rating. Unlike the Gadjradj et al study, which included only prospective studies, this review incorporated level 4 retrospective cohorts. The reason for greater initial disability among fusion recipients was unclear, limiting generalization. Identifying its causes could help reserve the more morbid fusion operation for patients likely to benefit. The findings nevertheless support offering D + F, especially with greater baseline disability. Given those methodological concerns, the present review rates the evidence Low and makes a Conditional recommendation to consider D and D + F equally for most DLS patients, while considering fusion for greater baseline disability and back pain.

document_sections.heading: Study Summary
document_sections.content: Blumenthal and colleagues described a prospective, single-center series of 40 patients aged 50-80 years with Grade I spondylolisthesis, neurogenic claudication and stability defined by less than 3 mm flexion-extension motion and no severe mechanical back pain. All received D. Baseline imaging assessed slip, disc height, facet angle, flexion-extension segmental motion and sagittal rotation. During mean follow-up of 3.6 years, 15 (37%) underwent reoperation for mechanical back pain presumed to reflect instability at the index level. Reoperation occurred in 45% with disc height >6.5 mm, 39% with facet angle >50°, and 54% with motion at the slipped segment of more than 1.25 mm. The rate was 75% when all three factors were present and 0% when none was present. Although data were collected prospectively at one center, the 40 patients were not enrolled consecutively; the review consequently describes the study as appearing to be a retrospective single-center study with prospectively collected data. It had one treatment arm and no comparator. Disc height and facet angle were measured on preoperative CT; other variables came from lateral lumbar radiographs. CT disc-height measurements may be less dependable than X-ray measurements for evaluating mechanical loading. The authors did not justify stepwise multivariate forward-selection logistic regression with threshold P-value of 0.35. Mean time to reoperation follow-up, described as 3.6 years, did not appear prespecified. Reoperation was the principal efficacy endpoint, but criteria for undertaking it were absent. Minimally invasive surgery was not evaluated. These methodological issues restrict generalizability, and the evidence level was described as very low. The findings suggest segmental motion >1.25 mm, disc height >6.5 mm and facet angle >50° as important reoperation-risk markers after D in DLS: the rate was 75% with all three, while at least one marker was associated with rates of 39%–54%. Small size and nonstandardized outcomes further limit application. Surgeons should nevertheless examine preoperative images for instability indicators when deciding whether fusion might benefit a patient. The present review calls this a level 4 retrospective study, assigns evidence quality Low and gives a Conditional recommendation that radiographic evaluation may help determine when fusion should accompany planned D for DLS.

document_sections.heading: Discussion
document_sections.content: Across the three RCT’s, final ODI did not differ between D + F and D. The North American SLIP trial used the SF36 physical component as its primary endpoint and reported greater improvement after D + F; that measure was not commonly used in the European RCT’s. SLIP and NORDSTEN-DS reported more index-level reoperations after D, whereas SSSS reported no reoperation difference. Inconsistent use of midline-sparing decompression and other nonstandardized surgical techniques complicates comparisons. The two recent meta-analyses reached opposing conclusions, although one reported a greater magnitude of functional improvement with D + F. Together, the mixed results do not establish a single efficacy conclusion for all surgically treated DLS. The condition likely includes stable, unstable and potentially unstable cases after D. D is suitable for many patients, but in a subset it may cause or worsen instability and lead to index-level reoperation.

document_sections.heading: Conclusion
document_sections.content: Considering these publications together, the review makes a strong recommendation that either D or D + F can be considered for surgical treatment of DLS. It remains uncertain which individual patients need each approach, although possible clinical and imaging indicators of instability risk have been proposed. Further research should clarify patient, imaging and technical predictors of postoperative instability so that the additional morbidity of fusion can be reserved for patients whose instability warrants it.
